summary:
Fire behaves fundamentally differently in microgravity than it does on Earth. In spacecraft, the absence of natural buoyancy changes flame propagation, smoke movement, oxygen transport, and fire suppression behaviour. These differences create serious safety challenges for astronauts and future lunar and Martian missions.

FlameLens is an interactive, research-driven decision-support platform that transforms fragmented microgravity combustion research into accessible fire-safety intelligence.

The platform brings together a curated catalogue of 22 space-combustion experiment records, interactive multi-criteria fire-risk rankings, side-by-side experimental comparisons, and an AI-powered assistant that generates research-grounded explanations. It also includes an interactive flame-behaviour simulator, spacecraft fire-safety guidance, and an educational learning module.

By combining scientific research, explainable analytical methods, interactive visualizations, and AI-assisted insights, FlameLens helps researchers, spacecraft engineers, mission planners, and students better understand combustion risks in space.

Our goal is to make decades of space-combustion research more accessible and useful for developing safer spacecraft and future human exploration missions.
details:
Problem Statement

Fire is one of the most critical hazards in human spaceflight. Unlike Earth, spacecraft operate in microgravity environments where natural buoyancy-driven convection is significantly reduced or absent.

As a result:

  • Flames can develop spherical, diffusion-dominated structures rather than familiar upward flames.
  • Smoke and combustion products do not naturally rise and may follow spacecraft ventilation pathways.
  • Low-speed airflow can influence flame propagation in unexpected ways.
  • Certain combustion processes, including low-temperature cool-flame reactions, may continue beyond visible flame extinction.
  • Future lunar and Martian habitats introduce additional challenges involving atmospheric pressure, oxygen concentration, and material flammability.

Although NASA and other space agencies have conducted extensive combustion experiments, their findings are distributed across research archives, technical reports, and scientific publications.

There is a need for an accessible platform that organizes these findings and helps users interpret their implications for spacecraft fire safety.

Our Solution: FlameLens

FlameLens is a unified research and decision-support platform designed to make microgravity combustion knowledge accessible, interactive, and actionable.

It combines structured experimental information, transparent risk-ranking methodologies, comparative analytics, and AI-assisted research explanations within a single application.

Core Features

1. Unified Microgravity Experiment Catalogue

A searchable catalogue containing 22 curated combustion experiment records. Users can explore experiments based on space agency, research platform, fuel type, gravity environment, and experimental conditions.

The catalogue includes detailed experiment information, findings, fire-risk implications, source references, and CSV/JSON export functionality.

2. Interactive Fire-Risk Ranking Engine

An explainable multi-criteria scoring system that assigns configurable 0–100 heuristic scores to experimental records.

The default weighting considers:

  • Fire-risk severity: 40%
  • Exploration relevance: 30%
  • Evidence strength: 15%
  • Suppression insight value: 15%

Users can adjust the weighting parameters and observe how experiment rankings change through interactive visualizations.

3. Multi-Experiment Comparison Engine

Allows users to compare two to four experiments simultaneously, examining differences in oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, fuel materials, and other experimental conditions.

Interactive charts and comparative summaries help users understand the potential engineering implications of different combustion environments.

4. AI-Powered Fire-Safety Assistant

An AI-assisted research interface that uses the curated experiment records as its evidence context.

It supports different audiences, including astronauts, engineers, and students, with English and Hindi responses. The assistant is designed to reference relevant experiment identifiers, communicate uncertainty, and encourage verification against original research.

A deterministic rule-based fallback is available when the external AI service is unavailable.

5. Interactive Flame Dynamics Simulator

A physics-education simulator that demonstrates how flame morphology changes across Earth gravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, and microgravity.

Users can explore the effects of gravity and airflow on combustion behaviour through interactive visualizations.

6. Spacecraft Fire-Safety Guide

A structured educational resource covering combustion physics, ignition, materials, atmospheric conditions, detection, suppression, and emergency-response considerations.

7. Interactive Learning Module

An eight-question knowledge assessment that explains answers and connects users with relevant experiment records. Users can also generate a personalized completion certificate.

8. Space Agency Research Profiles

Provides information about international space research programmes, relevant experimental platforms, ISS modules, and historical milestones in spacecraft combustion research.

Technology Stack

  • Frontend: Next.js 14 and React
  • Programming Language: TypeScript
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS
  • Data Visualization: Recharts
  • Interactive Graphics: HTML5 Canvas and Three.js
  • AI Integration: Anthropic Claude API
  • Backend: Next.js API Routes
  • Deployment: Netlify
  • Offline Support: Progressive Web Application capabilities

Methodology

FlameLens organizes experimental information into a standardized structure covering fuel materials, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity conditions, experimental findings, and safety implications.

These records are used by the experiment discovery interface, the configurable heuristic ranking engine, the comparison module, and the AI-assisted explanation system.

The ranking methodology is transparent and configurable rather than presented as a scientifically validated prediction model. Similarly, the AI assistant is a research-support tool and not a replacement for qualified spacecraft safety engineering.

Expected Impact

FlameLens aims to:

  • Improve access to fragmented microgravity combustion research.
  • Support comparative analysis of spacecraft fire experiments.
  • Help researchers identify potentially important fire-risk conditions.
  • Make space-combustion research easier to understand through interactive visualizations.
  • Support educational awareness of fire safety in human space exploration.
  • Contribute to research-informed discussions around safer lunar, Martian, and orbital habitats.

Future Scope

Future development could include deeper integration with NASA Physical Sciences Informatics datasets, automated scientific literature extraction, expanded experimental coverage, validation of the heuristic ranking methodology against domain-expert assessments, and more advanced physics-based simulations.

FlameLens is an independent research and decision-support prototype. It is not a certified spacecraft fire-safety system and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA or any international space agency.
